name: EchoStar: The Harvest That Ate Itself
deck: EchoStar's collapse shows the terminal problem of the harvest: when the captive base shrinks faster than returns can be extracted, the balance sheet fails and the franchise dies.
core_bet: EchoStar is the clearest proof that the harvest has a hard limit. Pay-TV subscribers fell from 6.998M to 6.391M between FY2025 and Q2 2026 as price increases exceeded perceived value; the company carried $7.321B in current debt maturities against $1.883B in liquidity, forcing substantial-doubt going-concern language. The strategy that once generated cash—harvesting legacy satellite pay-TV while building toward 5G—failed when the subscriber base shrank faster than the 5G buildout could replace it. Ultimately EchoStar abandoned its facilities-based network ambition and moved customer traffic to AT&T. The spectrum and orbital slots retain asset value; the franchise does not.

mechanism: EchoStar built its cash harvest on a simple model: extract recurring revenue from millions of legacy satellite pay-TV subscribers (DISH TV and SLING TV at 6.998M at year-end 2025) while building a new facilities-based 5G network to replace declining video subscriber economics. The model required simultaneously milking an aging customer base through price increases while burning billions to build out a wireless network that could eventually earn back the investment. This is the harvest model at its purest: short-term extraction subsidizes long-term optionality, all while returning cash to shareholders.

The problem emerged in 2025-2026 when the subscriber base shrank faster than management had modeled. Pay-TV subscribers fell 607,000 in just two quarters (6.998M to 6.391M), accelerating the pace of decline. Price increases, intended to extract more per customer, actually accelerated the churn. Customers were not switching to EchoStar's own 5G service—they were leaving the ecosystem entirely for streaming, wireless-only, and broadband alternatives. Meanwhile, the 5G buildout that was supposed to replace pay-TV economics had failed its core strategic test: management migrated all customer traffic off the company's own 5G network to AT&T by November 2025, abandoning the facilities-based ambition entirely. The network, built at enormous capital cost, could not compete with AT&T's established infrastructure. EchoStar went from a company building its own network to a company renting bandwidth from AT&T while paying off debt for infrastructure that no longer served its purpose.

The balance-sheet arithmetic then became brutal. FY2025 ended with $7.321B in current debt maturities (including $2.0B in July 2026, $1.377B in August 2026, and $2.750B in December 2026) against only $1.883B in cash and equivalents. The company's FY2025 annual report stated substantial doubt about the ability to continue as a going concern. Operating losses totaled $(17.723)B in FY2025 (driven by write-downs on impaired infrastructure investments), while the company was still generating $15B in revenue. Net losses were $(14.497)B. This is harvest economics collapsing in real time: you cannot harvest cash from a shrinking base fast enough to service debt taken on to build infrastructure that failed. By Q2 2026, the company had deconsolidated substantially all of the Pay-TV segment (moving it off-balance-sheet), with the entities continuing only to lease capacity on EchoStar's satellite fleet—a shift that reflected legal bankruptcy proceedings and the end of the consolidated franchise story.
why_now: EchoStar's unwind is accelerating because the harvest model's fatal flaw has become visible: you cannot extract your way out of structural decline. For years, companies can raise prices on captive customers, keeping cash flow positive even as the base shrinks. But there is an inflection point where price elasticity breaks—when the annual price increase exceeds the value perceived by customers. At that point, subscribers leave not gradually but in waves. EchoStar hit that point in 2025-2026. Meanwhile, the capex-heavy pivot to 5G was supposed to hedge the pay-TV decline, but the company could not compete with AT&T's installed network and backing. The moment when capex-driven optionality meets an accelerating subscriber cliff, the harvest model fails. There is no positive cash flow to show, no optionality to harvest, only debt maturity walls and the need for emergency restructuring.
who_pays: The remaining EchoStar customers—DISH TV and SLING TV subscribers who stayed through years of price increases and now face service disruption and forced migration. The company's employees, many of whom worked on the 5G buildout that was ultimately abandoned. The suppliers and contractors who relied on EchoStar as a customer and now face payment risk. The communities that relied on satellite connectivity, enterprise, and government services through Hughes. The broader ecosystem of small pay-TV players and rural broadband providers that looked to EchoStar as a technology and competitive option.
who_profits: Short-term: creditors holding EchoStar debt, who will negotiate recovery through restructuring. Private equity or larger telecom players (AT&T most directly) who can acquire EchoStar's spectrum, orbital slots, Hughes assets, and customer contracts at distressed prices. Creditors and financial buyers who monetize the underlying assets (spectrum, satellite capacity) separately from the consumer franchise. No one profits from the consumer franchise itself—it is worthless because it is unprofitable and shrinking. The profits come from the salvage value of assets when stripped from the failed operating company.
tension: The harvest model's structural paradox is fully exposed here: extracting cash from a shrinking base requires raising prices to offset volume decline. But raising prices accelerates the departure of marginal customers. At scale, this creates a death spiral. EchoStar tried to hedge by building 5G, but 5G failed because the company could not compete with established carriers and had to move traffic to AT&T anyway. The company then faced a debt wall ($7.321B in current maturities) with a shrinking cash base and no optionality left to harvest. The real cost is borne by customers who lose service, employees who lose jobs, and suppliers who lose a customer. The balance sheet loses paper value through write-downs. But the asset loss—spectrum, orbital slots, and infrastructure—has already been spent.
surprising_part: The most striking aspect is that EchoStar generated $15B in revenue while losing $14.5B net and carrying $26B+ in total debt. Revenue was not the problem; returns were. The company had sufficient scale to generate top-line dollars but insufficient profitability and cash generation to service the leverage taken on to fund growth. This is the opposite of typical insolvency. It is not lack of revenue; it is structural unprofitability and negative returns on past capital invested. When a harvesting company's base shrinks faster than it can raise prices, the leverage becomes a trap—the debt was taken on assuming revenue growth or margin expansion that never materialized. The company is caught between price-sensitive customers leaving and fixed debt obligations that cannot be escaped.
one_sentence: EchoStar went from harvesting legacy pay-TV cash to fund a wireless future—to discovering neither cash harvest nor wireless future could sustain the debt, forcing the company into bankruptcy and asset liquidation.
societal_stake: This is a story about infrastructure stranded value and the human cost when extraction strategies fail. EchoStar's satellite and spectrum assets are still strategically important—they have value. But that value cannot be realized through the consumer franchise. Millions of pay-TV customers are losing access, rural communities are losing satellite connectivity options, and the workforce deployed to build the 5G network is being disbanded. The satellite infrastructure that once connected remote America is being picked apart by financial buyers. This shows how harvest-driven strategy, when it fails, leaves not just companies but entire infrastructure and communities damaged.

evidence.fact: FY2025 Pay-TV subscribers: DISH TV 5.022M, SLING TV 1.976M, total 6.998M
Q2 2026 Pay-TV subscribers: DISH TV 4.684M, SLING TV 1.707M, total 6.391M (607K decline in 2 quarters)
FY2025 current debt maturities: $7.321B against cash and equivalents of $1.883B; debt maturities included $2.0B July 2026, $1.377B August 2026, $2.750B December 2026

FY2025 annual report stated substantial doubt about company and subsidiaries' ability to continue as a going concern; did not have necessary cash, projected future cash flows, or committed financing to fund obligations over next twelve months
FY2025 financial results: revenue $15.005B, operating loss $(17.723)B, net loss $(14.497)B; all driven by write-downs and impairments on infrastructure investments
By November 2025, customer traffic was migrated off company's own 5G network to AT&T; facilities-based wireless buildout was abandoned; company shifted to hybrid MNO model using AT&T infrastructure

Q2 2026: substantially all Pay-TV segment was deconsolidated; deconsolidated entities continue to lease satellite capacity from EchoStar but are no longer in consolidated financials, reflecting bankruptcy restructuring
By contrast, Charter ended 2025 with $94.6B principal debt but also $54.774B full-year revenue and $5.004B free cash flow; managed pay-TV decline through broadband and mobile growth
Q2 2026: Charter had 29.4M Internet customers (down 172K quarter), 12.5M mobile lines (up 406K), 31.5M customer relationships; shows sustainable churn management through diversification
